c.pop: General Luna (main hub): 22,853 (2020 census); whole Siargao Island: ~117,000
c.tagline: Where the waves end and the island wilderness begins

card: Cash is king in Siargao. Most homestays, tricycles, habal-habal drivers, and small eateries are cash-only; only larger resorts and a handful of restaurants in General Luna accept cards. ATMs are limited to a few machines in General Luna and Dapa and can run out of cash on weekends. GCash mobile wallet is widely accepted as a cash alternative.

taxi.color: n/a — no metered taxis exist on the island
taxi.fare: Tricycle in-town: ₱20-30/person day, ₱50/person night; habal-habal short trip (5-10km): ₱50-100; medium (10-30km): ₱100-200; long (30km+): ₱300-400/person
taxi.fareNote: All fares are informally negotiated flat-rate by distance, not metered — agree on price before boarding. Renting a scooter (₱350-600/day) is the most common way solo travelers get around.

emergency.police: 911 (national emergency hotline) or General Luna Municipal Police Station
emergency.medical: Coastal Community Hospital / Lopez General Luna Community Hospital for basic care; serious cases are referred to Surigao City or Cebu
emergency.note: 911 works nationally but response times are slow due to limited island infrastructure. Reef cuts and scooter accidents are the most common tourist injuries — travel insurance with medevac coverage is strongly recommended.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

walk: General Luna's town center and the Cloud 9 boardwalk are walkable/bikeable, but Siargao overall is not a walking destination — attractions are spread across the island, so most visitors rely on rented scooters, habal-habal, or tricycles. Roads outside the main strip can be unpaved, especially after rain.

safety.safety: Generally safe for solo travelers, including women — Siargao has a large, established surfer and digital-nomad community used to visitors. Main risks are road accidents on rented scooters and ocean hazards (reef cuts, rip currents) rather than crime.
safety.crime: Violent crime against tourists is rare. Petty theft from resort rooms and parked bikes does occur — use accommodations with lockers/safes and avoid leaving belongings unattended on beaches.

hood_landmark.Cloud 9: Cloud 9 surf break and wooden watchtower

avoid.reason: Don't leave belongings unattended on beaches, and take care on General Luna's dark, pothole-strewn roads at night where drunk scooter accidents are the main hazard.

hood_desc: The island's main tourist hub — General Luna ('GL') is where most restaurants, bars, dive shops, and accommodation cluster along the coastal road leading to the Cloud 9 boardwalk.
The world-famous surf break and its wooden boardwalk over the reef — a compact strip of surf camps, board rentals, and beachfront cafes built right around the wave.
A quieter, greener area just north of Cloud 9, known for the AFAM sunset bridge and rice-paddy backroads, favored by high-end hideaway resorts and long-term nomads.
A remote, uncrowded beach on the northeastern coast, roughly an hour from General Luna over rough roads — popular with surfers seeking less-crowded breaks.
The functional gateway town — home to the ferry port connecting to Surigao City and close to Sayak Airport, with basic lodging and eateries for transiting travelers.

water.note: Drink bottled or refilled filtered water; island tap water is not reliably potable.

transit.sys: No formal public transit system exists on Siargao
transit.hours: Tricycles and habal-habal generally operate 6am-10pm; night rides cost more and become scarce late
transit.pay: Cash only, paid directly to the driver, fare negotiated up front
transit.map: n/a — no route map; drivers are hailed on the street or arranged via accommodation/Facebook groups
transit.note: Most independent travelers rent their own scooter (₱350-600/day) for flexibility since tricycles don't run fixed routes.

transport.air: Fly into Sayak Airport (IAO), connecting via Cebu (Cebgo, Philippine Airlines, Sunlight Air) or Clark; limited/seasonal direct Manila service.
transport.train: None — no rail service to Mindanao/Siargao
transport.bus: No direct bus to Siargao; buses/vans connect Surigao City to other Mindanao points, then ferry to Dapa
transport.ferry: Fastcraft/RORO ferries run from Surigao City to Dapa port, roughly 3 daily departures, journey 2-4 hours
transport.car: No car rental culture on the island — nearly everyone gets around by rented scooter, habal-habal, or tricycle; some operators offer private van transfers

airport.name: Sayak Airport
airport.distance: ~40 km / 45-60 minutes by road to General Luna and Cloud 9
airport.transport: Shared van (~$5-7, 45-60 min), private van (~$35-45), or pre-arranged hotel transfer

net.m: Good coverage in General Luna and Cloud 9, weaker in remote areas like Pacifico and Sohoton
net.w: Most resorts, cafes, and restaurants in General Luna and Cloud 9 offer free wifi, though speed and reliability vary
net.fwn: Free wifi common at accommodations and cafes in the main tourist strip
net.ap: Local SIM (Globe or Smart) recommended, sold in General Luna town

tip.s: Tipping is not deeply ingrained but increasingly appreciated in the tourism sector — rounding up or leaving 10% at restaurants is welcomed
tip.r: For habal-habal drivers, tour guides, surf instructors, and boat crews, a small tip (₱50-200) is customary and appreciated

food.name: Kinilaw
food.desc: Raw tuna or sailfish cured in coconut vinegar with calamansi, ginger, chilli, onion and often coconut milk; the Caraga answer to ceviche.

places.name: CEV Siargao
places.note: Kinilaw and ceviche shack using the day's catch from local fishermen; the island's specialist.

places.name: Emilias

places.name: Karagatan Siargao
places.note: Seafood-led kitchen where kinilaw is a fixture of the menu.

food.name: Sinuglaw
food.desc: Charcoal-grilled pork belly tossed through tuna kinilaw so the smoke and fat meet the sour vinegar cure; a Mindanao classic.

places.name: Mamas Grill
places.note: Roadside charcoal shack that locals and surfers queue at after sunset.

places.name: Emilias
places.area: General Luna, off the main road

places.name: CEV Siargao
places.note: Cured-fish specialists who also handle the grilled-pork pairing well.

food.desc: Tuna, squid, prawns, crab, lapu-lapu grouper or milkfish cooked over charcoal and served with a soy-calamansi and chilli dipping sauce.

places.name: Mamas Grill

places.name: Catangnan BBQ

food.name: Lechon and pork barbecue sticks
food.desc: Whole roast pig at fiestas, and every day the sweet soy-marinated pork skewers that Filipinos grill on the roadside from late afternoon.

places.name: Catangnan BBQ
places.note: The spot for Filipino sweet-sauce barbecue done properly.

places.name: Mamas Grill
places.note: Pork sticks alongside the seafood; go early before the good cuts sell out.

places.name: Dapa Public Market

food.name: Ginataang seafood
food.desc: Siargao is coconut country, so fish, prawns, crab, squash and greens are stewed in fresh coconut milk with ginger, chilli and turmeric.

places.name: Emilias
places.area: General Luna, off the main road
places.note: Home-cooked coconut stews of the sort island families actually eat.

places.name: Karagatan Siargao
places.note: Coconut-based seafood dishes served in a relaxed open-sided space.

places.name: Dapa Public Market
places.note: Surrounding carinderias ladle ginataang over rice for a few hundred pesos.

food.name: Sayongsong
food.desc: A Caraga sweet: sticky rice with coconut milk and muscovado steamed in a cone of banana leaf, eaten warm as a mid-morning snack.

places.name: Dapa Public Market
places.note: Vendors sell the cones fresh in the morning; ask for them by name.

places.name: General Luna Public Market
places.note: Native-snack stalls with sayongsong, suman and bibingka.

food.name: Buko juice
food.desc: Young coconut cracked open and drunk with a straw, then the soft jelly flesh scooped out; the default island thirst-quencher.

places.name: Cloud 9 boardwalk
places.note: Coconut vendors set up along the boardwalk through the surf sessions.

places.name: Shaka Siargao
places.note: Famous smoothie-bowl cafe that also does coconut and fresh tropical juices.

places.name: Dapa Public Market
places.note: Coconuts by the sack at market prices, opened for you on the spot.

food.name: Tuba
food.desc: Coconut palm sap collected at dawn and left to ferment into a cloudy, tangy palm wine; sweet when fresh, sharp and strong by evening.

places.name: Dapa Public Market
places.note: Tuba gatherers sell straight from plastic jugs in the morning.

places.name: Emilias

places.note: Local dining room where asking about tuba usually produces some.

places.name: Catangnan BBQ

landmarks: Cloud 9
The Philippines' most famous surf break, a barrelling reef wave off General Luna watched from an iconic three-tiered wooden boardwalk tower.
Magpupungko Rock Pools
Crystal-clear natural tidal pools framed by dramatic boulders at Pilar, perfect for swimming and cliff-jumping at low tide.
Sugba Lagoon
A jade-green lagoon enclosed by jungle limestone hills near Del Carmen, reached by boat through the Philippines' largest mangrove forest.
Daku Island
The largest of the tri-island hopping trio, a laid-back isle of coconut palms, a fishing village and a long ribbon of powdery white sand.
Guyam Island
A tiny postcard islet of leaning palms and white sand you can circle on foot in minutes, the classic Siargao photo stop.
Naked Island
A bare, dazzling sandbar rising from turquoise shallows, famous for having nothing on it at all except perfect swimming water.
Maasin River
A lazy palm-fringed river made famous by its bent coconut-tree rope swing, paddled by kayak or bamboo raft through emerald scenery.
Sohoton Cove (Bucas Grande)
A magical maze of lagoons, caves and stingless-jellyfish sanctuaries on neighbouring Bucas Grande Island, Siargao's finest boat day trip.
Coconut Mountain View Deck
A hilltop viewpoint above a rolling sea of thousands of coconut palms stretching to the horizon, Siargao's signature inland panorama.
Pacifico Beach
A quiet white-sand beach and mellow surf town on the island's north coast, beloved for uncrowded waves and sleepy barangay charm.

train.note: There is no railway on Siargao or anywhere in Mindanao. Arrive by air into Sayak airport near Del Carmen, about an hour from General Luna, or by ferry from Surigao City on the mainland.

bus.note: No international coaches. On the island, habal-habal motorbikes, tricycles and shared vans link Dapa port, Sayak airport and General Luna; there is no scheduled bus network. On the mainland, Bachelor Express coaches connect Surigao City with Butuan, Davao and Cagayan de Oro for those travelling overland.

intl.to: Surigao City (Philippines) - fast craft, ~2h30, and slower ro-ro
intl.op: Fortune Angel / Montenegro Lines — tickets at Dapa port

intl.to: Dapa & Socorro, Bucas Grande (Philippines) - for the Sohoton lagoons
intl.op: local bangka operators — tickets at the pier

ferry.note: There are no international sailings. The Surigao crossing to Dapa port is the main sea route, with fast craft taking about two and a half hours and cheaper ro-ro ferries longer; sailings are suspended when a typhoon signal goes up, and Siargao sits in a typhoon-prone belt, so keep a spare day before onward flights. Boats to Bucas Grande and the Sohoton caves are day trips.

full.name: Britania Group of Islands
full.blurb: A scattering of small limestone islets in Surigao del Sur with turquoise water, reached by boat from mainland Mindanao.

full.name: Dinagat Islands
full.blurb: A rugged island province with rock formations, hidden lagoons, and beaches, reached by boat across the strait from Siargao.
